extracted.intended_audience: judges, administrative-law practitioners, and lawyers who litigate or advise on judicial review of agency action
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and limits for how courts should evaluate agency statutory interpretations and when (if ever) courts should defer to agencies under doctrines like Chevron, Mead, and Skidmore, in light of the Administrative Procedure Act (APA).

rubrics_metrics.name: APA §706 — reviewing court decides all relevant questions of law
rubrics_metrics.description: The APA requires that 'the reviewing court'—not the agency whose action it reviews—is to 'decide all relevant questions of law' and 'interpret . . . statutory provisions.' §706.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts must exercise independent legal judgment in statutory interpretation when reviewing agency action; they may not abdicate that duty by simply accepting an agency's view of what the statute means.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chevron deference (original two-step)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Chevron, a judge was required to adopt an agency’s interpretation of an ambiguous statute so long as the agency had a 'permissible construction of the statute.' See Chevron, 467 U.S. 837 (1984).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chevron commanded mechanical deference in many cases—requiring courts to treat agency 'permissible' readings as controlling rather than determining what the court itself would conclude. The opinion concludes that such automatic deference conflicts with the APA's command that courts decide legal questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambiguity is not a delegation of interpretive power
rubrics_metrics.description: An ambiguity is simply not a delegation of law-interpreting power. Chevron confuses the two.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should not presume that statutory ambiguity equals congressional intent to delegate interpretive authority to an agency; many ambiguities are unintentional and do not reflect a grant of authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courts must identify the statute's 'best reading' (independent judgment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every statute's meaning is fixed at the time of enactment ... courts use every tool at their disposal to determine the best reading of the statute and resolve the ambiguity — 'the reading the court would have reached' if no agency were involved. (Chevron, 467 U.S., at 843, n.11 quoted).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In agency cases as in any other, courts must deploy traditional tools of statutory construction to ascertain the single best meaning; a merely 'permissible' interpretation that is not the court's best reading is not enough to bind the court.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency expertise is persuasive but not binding (Skidmore)
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency's interpretation 'cannot bind a court,' but it may be especially informative 'to the extent it rests on factual premises within [the agency's] expertise.' Agencies have 'power to persuade, if lacking power to control.' Skidmore, 323 U.S. at 140.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should give respectful consideration to agency views (especially where grounded in agency expertise and factual premises) under a Skidmore-like 'power to persuade' analysis, but such views do not replace the court's independent statutory interpretation obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chevron 'step zero' / Mead threshold for deference
rubrics_metrics.description: Chevron applies only 'when it appears that Congress delegated authority to the agency generally to make rules carrying the force of law, and that the agency interpretation claiming deference was promulgated in the exercise of that authority.' Mead, 533 U.S. at 226–227. In practice, that largely limits Chevron to 'the fruits of notice-and-comment rulemaking or formal adjudication.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before considering deference, courts must determine whether Congress in fact delegated interpretive authority to the agency and whether the agency's interpretation was promulgated via a mode of decisionmaking (e.g., notice-and-comment or formal adjudication) that carries the force of law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural defects in agency action preclude deference
rubrics_metrics.description: Chevron does not apply where the regulation is 'procedurally defective'—that is, where the agency errs by failing to follow the correct procedures in issuing the regulation. Encino Motorcars, LLC v. Navarro, 579 U.S. 211, 220 (2016) (quoting Mead).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an agency failed to comply with required procedures (e.g., notice-and-comment where required), that procedural defect can defeat any claim that the agency's interpretation merits judicial deference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Major questions / deep economic and political significance exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Chevron does not apply if the question at issue is one of 'deep "economic and political significance."' King v. Burwell, 576 U.S. 473, 486 (2015). For such matters, the Court expects Congress to delegate authority 'expressly' if at all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an issue would have vast economic or political consequences, courts should not assume Congress intended to delegate interpretive authority implicitly; express congressional authorization is required for agency control over such major questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other categorical limits on deference
rubrics_metrics.description: The Court has declined to apply Chevron to agency interpretations of judicial review provisions (Adams Fruit Co.), to statutory schemes not administered by the agency seeking deference (Epic Systems), and has shown mixed signals about application where statutes have criminal applications (compare Abramski v. United States with Babbitt v. Sweet Home).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts must consider context-specific categorical limits (type of statute, which agency administers it, criminal implications, interpretation of judicial-review provisions) before affording deference; these are independent constraints apart from the Mead/step-zero inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambiguity as a concept is indeterminate and unworkable
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The defining feature of [Chevron's] framework is the identification of statutory ambiguity, which requires deference at the doctrine's second step. But the concept of ambiguity has always evaded meaningful definition.' 'How clear is clear?' (quoting Justice Scalia).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because 'ambiguity' can be viewed differently by different judges, basing a deference regime on that indeterminate concept produces inconsistent and arbitrary results; a workable rule cannot rest on such an impressionistic test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stare decisis factors for overruling precedent
rubrics_metrics.description: Stare decisis considerations—'the quality of [the precedent's] reasoning, the workability of the rule it established, . . . and reliance on the decision'—are the relevant factors in deciding whether to retain or overrule a precedent. Knick v. Township of Scott, 588 U.S. 180, 203 (2019) (quoting Janus).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When these factors (poor reasoning, unworkability, and insufficient reliance benefits) weigh against a precedent, the Court may overrule it; mere reliance on an erroneous precedent does not constitute the special justification needed to retain it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency inconsistency and reliance interests
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Chevron, a statutory ambiguity can become a license authorizing an agency to change positions as much as it likes, with '[u]nexplained inconsistency' being 'at most . . . a reason for holding an interpretation to be . . . arbitrary and capricious.' Brand X, 545 U.S. at 981.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deference regimes that permit agencies to shift interpretations freely undermine reliance interests and legal stability; courts should police arbitrary or unexplained agency reversals under APA arbitrary-and-capricious review rather than surrender interpretive authority.
